instruction: Run one command over every matching file, batching them efficiently.
context: find -exec: terminating with + batches as many paths as fit into one invocation, while \; runs the command once per file. The + form is dramatically faster but requires {} to be the last argument.

instruction: List files modified more recently than a reference file.
context: find: -newer compares modification time against another file, which avoids guessing a -mtime day count. -newerct with a date string takes a literal timestamp instead.

instruction: Find files not modified in the last thirty days.
context: find: -mtime counts in 24-hour periods, where +30 means strictly more than thirty and -30 means less. A bare 30 means exactly the thirty-first day, which is almost never what is intended.

instruction: Find files changed in the last ten minutes.
context: find: -mmin is the minute-granularity counterpart to -mtime, and the leading minus means less than. This is the usual way to see what a build just touched.

instruction: Search a tree while skipping node_modules entirely.
context: find -prune stops descent into a matched directory, and it must be paired with -o and an explicit -print because pruning otherwise suppresses the default print. Ordering of the expression matters.

instruction: Find files bigger than one hundred megabytes.
context: find -size: the suffix picks the unit, where M is mebibytes and c is bytes. With no suffix the unit is 512-byte blocks, which silently makes -size +100 mean fifty kilobytes.

instruction: List empty directories left behind by a cleanup.
context: find: -empty matches zero-byte files and directories with no entries, selected by the preceding -type. Adding -delete removes them, and find processes depth-first so nested empties clear in one pass.

instruction: List only the immediate subdirectories, not the whole tree.
context: find: -maxdepth 1 limits recursion to the starting directory's own entries, and it must appear before other tests to avoid a warning. -mindepth 1 suppresses the starting directory itself.

instruction: Audit a tree for world-writable files.
context: find -perm: a leading minus means all of these bits are set, ignoring the others, while a leading slash means any of them. A bare mode requires an exact match and misses most real cases.

instruction: Safely pass filenames containing spaces to another command.
context: find -print0 separates paths with NUL rather than newline, and xargs -0 reads that form. Without the pair, filenames containing spaces or newlines are split into fragments.

instruction: Delete old temporary files in place.
context: find -delete removes matches without spawning rm, but it implies -depth and silently ignores anything placed after it in the expression. Always run the same expression with -print first.

instruction: Find which subdirectories are consuming the most space.
context: du: --max-depth=1 reports each immediate child rather than every nested directory, and -h uses unit suffixes. sort -h understands those suffixes, which plain sort -n does not.

instruction: Find which subdirectories are consuming the most space on macOS.
context: du: BSD du spells the depth limit -d and does not accept the GNU --max-depth= form. macOS sort does support -h, so the human-readable ordering still works.

instruction: Report actual file sizes rather than allocated disk blocks.
context: du: by default the total counts allocated blocks, so many small files report more than their contents. --apparent-size sums the logical sizes instead, matching what ls reports.

instruction: Diagnose a disk-full error when there is clearly free space.
context: df: -i reports inode usage rather than bytes, which is the explanation when writes fail at apparently low utilization. -h formats the counts with unit suffixes.

instruction: Find which process is holding port 8080.
context: lsof: -i filters to network files and -sTCP:LISTEN narrows to listeners rather than established connections. -n skips DNS resolution and -P skips port-name lookup, which makes it return instantly.

instruction: Find space held by deleted files that a process still has open.
context: lsof: +L1 lists files with a link count below one, meaning they are unlinked but still open, so their blocks are not freed until the holder exits. This explains df and du disagreeing.

instruction: Find what is keeping a filesystem busy so it will not unmount.
context: lsof: +D searches a directory recursively, which is thorough but slow, while +d checks only its immediate contents. fuser -m is the faster alternative for the unmount case.

instruction: List every listening TCP socket with its owning process.
context: ss: -t is TCP, -l is listening only, -n skips name resolution, and -p shows the owning process, which requires root to see other users' entries. -u adds UDP.

instruction: Show established connections to a specific port.
response: ss -tn state established '( dport = :443 or sport = :443 )'
context: ss accepts a filter expression after the options, where dport and sport are destination and source port. The state keyword replaces the -l flag with any TCP state name.

instruction: List the ten processes using the most memory.
context: ps: -o picks the output columns and --sort with a leading minus orders descending. rss is resident set size in kilobytes; head takes eleven lines because the first is the header.

instruction: See the complete command line of a running process, not the truncated form.
context: ps: args is the full command line where comm is only the executable name. --no-headers suits piping, and ww disables the terminal-width truncation in the BSD-style syntax.

instruction: Find the PID of a process by matching its full command line.
context: pgrep: -f matches against the entire command line rather than just the process name, which is required for interpreted scripts. -a prints the matched command alongside the PID.

instruction: Ask a process to reload its configuration rather than killing it.
context: pkill sends SIGTERM by default; naming a signal changes it, and HUP conventionally means reload. Preview the target set with the identical pgrep invocation before sending anything.

instruction: Force-terminate a process that is ignoring a normal stop request.
context: kill: the default signal is 15 (TERM), which a process can catch to shut down cleanly. Signal 9 (KILL) cannot be caught or ignored, so buffers are lost and temporary files are left behind.

instruction: Preview exactly what a mirroring sync would change before running it.
context: rsync: -n is the dry run and prints the transfer list without touching anything. --delete removes destination files absent from the source, so previewing it is not optional.

instruction: Copy the contents of a directory rather than the directory itself.
context: rsync: a trailing slash on the source means copy its contents into the destination, while omitting it creates a subdirectory of that name inside the destination. This is the single most common rsync mistake.

instruction: Transfer a large file over a flaky link so it can resume.
context: rsync: --partial keeps a partially transferred file so a rerun resumes instead of restarting. --inplace writes directly to the destination file rather than a temporary copy, halving the space needed.

instruction: Sync a project while skipping build output and version control.
context: rsync: --exclude is repeatable and its pattern is matched against the path relative to the transfer root. A trailing slash restricts the match to directories; --exclude-from reads a list from a file.

instruction: Extract an archive without its redundant top-level directory.
context: tar: --strip-components removes that many leading path elements from each member during extraction, which flattens the usual project-1.0/ wrapper directory. -C selects the destination directory.

instruction: Archive a project while leaving out the build directory.
context: tar: --exclude must appear before the paths being archived in GNU tar, because options are processed in order. The pattern matches path components anywhere in the tree.

instruction: Show a file's permissions in octal form.
context: stat -c takes a format string where %a is the octal access mode, %n the name, %U the owner, and %s the size in bytes. GNU spells this -c and BSD spells it -f with different specifiers.

instruction: Make a script executable without altering its other permissions.
context: chmod: symbolic modes adjust bits relative to the current state, so +x adds execute for all classes filtered by umask. An octal mode like 755 sets every bit at once and discards what was there.

instruction: Recursively fix a tree so directories are traversable but files do not become executable.
context: chmod: capital X sets the execute bit only on directories and on files that already have execute somewhere, unlike lowercase x which sets it on every file. This is the correct recursive repair.

instruction: Give a whole directory tree to a service user and group.
context: chown: the colon form sets owner and group together, and a bare trailing colon uses the user's login group. -h changes symlinks themselves rather than their targets.

instruction: Replace an existing symlink so it points somewhere new.
context: ln: -s makes a symbolic link, -f replaces an existing target, and -n is essential when the target is already a symlink to a directory, otherwise the new link is created inside it.

instruction: Copy a tree preserving timestamps, ownership, and symlinks.
context: cp: -a is archive mode, equivalent to -dR --preserve=all, so links stay links and metadata survives. Plain -r follows symlinks and resets timestamps to now.

instruction: Copy files only when the source is newer than the destination.
context: cp: -u skips a copy when the destination exists and is not older, which makes reruns cheap. It compares modification times only, so a same-timestamp change is not detected.

instruction: Copy a binary into place with the right mode, creating the directory if needed.
context: install combines copy, chmod, and directory creation in one atomic-ish step. -D creates missing parent directories of the destination and -m sets the mode directly, avoiding a separate chmod.

instruction: Create a safe temporary working directory.
context: mktemp -d creates a directory with a unique name and mode 700, atomically, which avoids the symlink race of picking a name yourself. The path is printed on stdout for capture.

instruction: Resolve a command's path through every symlink to the real file.
context: readlink: -f canonicalizes the whole path and requires all but the last component to exist, while -e requires every component to exist and -m requires none. Plain readlink prints only the immediate target.

instruction: Re-run a status command every couple of seconds and highlight what changed.
context: watch: -n sets the interval in seconds and -d highlights the differences between refreshes. Quoting the command is required so the shell does not expand it once at start.

instruction: Give a command a hard time limit and kill it if it hangs.
context: timeout: the first duration is the deadline after which TERM is sent, and -k adds a grace period before an unblockable KILL. It exits 124 on timeout, which scripts can test for.

instruction: Start a long job that survives the terminal closing.
context: nohup makes the process ignore SIGHUP so a closing terminal does not kill it. Redirecting both streams is still needed, otherwise output lands in nohup.out in the current directory.

instruction: Find which config file a program is actually reading.
context: strace: -e trace= filters to a syscall group, -f follows forked children, and -o writes to a file so the program's own output stays readable. openat is the modern replacement for open.

instruction: Run a heavy backup without starving the rest of the machine.
context: nice -n raises the scheduling niceness, where 19 is the lowest CPU priority. ionice -c 3 sets the idle I/O class, so the job only reads when nothing else wants the disk.

instruction: Identify what a file actually is when its extension is missing or wrong.
context: file inspects magic bytes rather than trusting the name. -b omits the filename prefix for clean piping, and --mime-type reports the type in MIME form instead of prose.

instruction: List a directory with the most recently modified files last.
context: ls: -t sorts by modification time newest first and -r reverses it, which puts the newest at the bottom next to the prompt. -u sorts by access time and -c by inode change time instead.

instruction: List files largest first with readable sizes.
context: ls: capital -S sorts by size descending, which is unrelated to lowercase -s that prints allocated blocks. -h adds unit suffixes and only affects the display, not the ordering.

instruction: Check whether a filesystem is mounted read-only.
context: findmnt queries the kernel mount table in a structured way: -o picks columns, -n drops the header, and giving a path reports the filesystem containing it. Plain mount output requires parsing prose.

instruction: Find which process is listening on a port on macOS.
context: macOS ships no ss, so lsof -i is the way to inspect listening sockets. The flags match the Linux lsof exactly, and netstat -an on macOS cannot attribute sockets to processes.

instruction: List processes by memory use on macOS.
context: ps: BSD ps has no --sort, so -m sorts by memory and -r sorts by CPU. The -o column names are otherwise the same as the GNU ones.

instruction: Batch a command over matching files on macOS.
context: BSD find supports the + terminator for batching just as GNU find does. What it lacks is -printf and the GNU-only -newermt shorthand, so those need -exec stat instead.
